question_text: If the coefficients of x⁹, x¹⁰, x¹¹ in the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ are in A.P., then prove that n² − 41n + 398 = 0.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — what the three coefficients are, what being in A.P. means once you divide by the middle one, the two ratio formulas you substitute, and how the algebra reaches n² − 41n + 398 = 0.
insider_note: The coefficient of x⁹ is ⁿC₉ — here the power IS the index, and shifting to ⁿC₈ proves a different equation. Write 2·ⁿC₁₀ = ⁿC₉ + ⁿC₁₁ and divide by the middle coefficient so the two ratios appear. The question asks only for the equation, and that is the whole answer: n² − 41n + 398 = 0 has discriminant 89, which is not a perfect square, so there is no whole number n for which those three coefficients are in A.P. Do not lose time trying to solve it.

steps.label: Name the three coefficients
steps.margin_note: First mark. The coefficient of x⁹ in (1 + x)ⁿ is ⁿC₉ — here the power of x IS the index, unlike the "r-th term" wording of the general question.
lines: The coefficients of x⁹, x¹⁰, x¹¹ in (1 + x)ⁿ are
ⁿC₉, ⁿC₁₀, ⁿC₁₁ and they are in A.P.

recall.must_convey: That the coefficients of x⁹, x¹⁰, x¹¹ are ⁿC₉, ⁿC₁₀, ⁿC₁₁.

steps.why: A coefficient of (1 + x)ⁿ is a binomial coefficient, and the coefficient of the r-th term carries r − 1, not r. Naming the three correctly is the step the rest of the answer depends on.
common_mistakes: Shifting the index and writing ⁿC₈, ⁿC₉, ⁿC₁₀ — that shift belongs to "r-th term" wording, not to "coefficient of xᵏ".
Treating x⁹, x¹⁰, x¹¹ as the 9th, 10th, 11th terms.

steps.label: Write the A.P. condition
steps.margin_note: Three numbers are in A.P. when the middle one is the average of the other two: 2·(middle) = (first) + (last). Divide through by the middle coefficient so the ratios appear.

recall.must_convey: That 2·ⁿC₁₀ = ⁿC₉ + ⁿC₁₁, and dividing by ⁿC₁₀ gives 2 = ⁿC₉/ⁿC₁₀ + ⁿC₁₁/ⁿC₁₀.

steps.why: Dividing by the middle coefficient turns three binomial coefficients into two RATIOS of consecutive coefficients, and those ratios have a one-line formula.
common_mistakes: Writing the A.P. condition as first + middle = last.
Not dividing by the middle term and trying to expand the factorials.

steps.label: Replace the ratios
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. With r = 10: ⁿC₉/ⁿC₁₀ = 10/(n − 9) and ⁿC₁₁/ⁿC₁₀ = (n − 10)/11.

recall.must_convey: That the two ratios are 10/(n − 9) and (n − 10)/11, so 2 = 10/(n − 9) + (n − 10)/11.
accept: n C nine by n C ten is ten by n minus nine and n C eleven by n C ten is n minus ten by eleven

steps.why: ⁿCᵣ/ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = (n − r + 1)/r and ⁿCᵣ₊₁/ⁿCᵣ = (n − r)/(r + 1) come straight from the factorial form; they replace every binomial coefficient by plain algebra in n and r.
common_mistakes: Inverting one of the two ratios.
Using (n − r)/r instead of (n − r + 1)/r for the lower ratio.

steps.label: Clear fractions and simplify
steps.margin_note: Fifth to seventh marks. Multiply through by 11(n − 9). The right side is 110 + (n − 10)(n − 9) = n² − 19n + 200.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying by 11(n − 9) gives 22n − 198 = 110 + (n − 10)(n − 9), and collecting terms gives n² − 41n + 398 = 0.

steps.why: Cross-multiplying once and collecting like terms is all that remains; the required equation is exactly what falls out, with nothing to guess.
common_mistakes: Getting +41n by moving terms to the wrong side.
